authors: Revilla, Sonia Aristin; Cutilli, Alessandro; Cambiaso, Eugenia; Rockx-Brouwer, Dedeke; Frederiks, Cynthia Lisanne; Falandt, Marc; Levato, Riccardo; Kranenburg, Onno; Lindemans, Caroline A; Coffer, Paul James; Peperzak, Victor; Mocholi, Enric; Cuenca, Marta

summary: The study compares how different 3D hydrogels—animal-derived Matrigel/BME versus synthetic nanofibrillar cellulose (NFC)—affect T cell and CAR-T cell activation, proliferation, and function. NFC, despite being stiffer, preserves (CAR-)T cell activation, proliferation, cytokine production, survival, and expansion, while Matrigel/BME dampen activation and induce murine Treg differentiation; short-term CAR-T cytotoxicity is similar across gels, but longer-term activation and proliferation are maintained only in NFC.
summary_mandm: Murine CD4+ T cells were obtained from B6-Foxp3 EGFP mouse lymph nodes and spleens, mechanically dissociated by pressing through a cell strainer, washed in MACS buffer (2% heat‑inactivated FBS, 2 mM EDTA in PBS), counted, and magnetically isolated with Miltenyi CD4 (L3T4) MicroBeads on LS Columns using a QuadroMACS separator. Human CD4+ T cells came from cord blood mononuclear cells prepared by Ficoll-Paque density gradient, cryopreserved, thawed, and enriched using the MagniSort Human CD4+ T Cell Enrichment Kit with BD IMag magnet. For encapsulation, NFC (GrowDex) was diluted to 0.25% w/v in medium and used at room temperature; Matrigel (Corning) and BME (Cultrex RGF Type 2) were diluted 1:1 in medium on ice and gelled at 37°C for 30 min; all cultures included IL-2 (typically 20 U/mL) and anti-CD3/CD28 (1 μg/mL) for 5 days (murine/human CD4+ T cells), with CAR-T stimulations using coated anti-CD3 (1.6 μg/mL) and soluble anti-CD28 (1 μg/mL). Embedded cells were recovered from NFC by enzymatic digestion with GrowDase (UPM Biomedicals) at 37°C for ~3 h (also 2 μg/mL GrowDase added with GolgiStop for intracellular staining), and from Matrigel/BME using Corning Cell Recovery Solution; all samples were passed through a 30 μm strainer prior to flow cytometry. CD20 CAR-T cells were generated from human PBMCs via gamma-retroviral transduction (Phoenix-Ampho; GALV env), after preactivation with OKT3 (anti-CD3, Miltenyi) and IL-2, expanded with CD3/CD28 Dynabeads and IL-2, and selected with neomycin; cytotoxicity assays used Daudi targets and 24 h co-culture in each gel, followed by gel digestion and flow cytometry.

title: Impact of Mixed-In Polyacrylic- and Phosphonate-Based Additives on Lime Mortar Microstructure.

raw_affiliation: Department of Geology, Ghent University, Krijgslaan 281/Building S8, B-9000 Ghent, Belgium.
summary: The study investigates how mixed-in aminotris(methylene phosphonic acid) (ATMP) and poly(acrylic acid) sodium salts (PAA) of different molecular weights alter the microstructure, porosity, carbonation behavior, and mechanical properties of lime mortars. Optimized dosages promote nanostructured CaCO3 (mesocrystals) and stabilize vaterite, enhancing strength via biomimetic toughening and improved CO2 diffusion, whereas excessive additive levels cause high air entrainment and reduced mechanical performance.
summary_mandm: Lime mortars (binder:aggregate 1:3 by volume) were prepared per EN 1015-11 using CL90-S hydrated lime and CEN standard quartz sand, with water adjusted by flow table to 165 ± 10 mm; ATMP and PAA (Mw 5100 and 2100) were dissolved in mix water at 100, 500, or 1000 ppm (by dry binder+aggregate mass). Mortars were cast in molds in two layers compacted with 25 tamper strokes per layer, topped with cotton gauze/filter paper and a 5 kg load for 3 h, then cured 5 days in mold and a further 2 days at 20 °C/95% RH followed by 21 or 83 days at 20 °C/65% RH; for STEM, inner-core binder was obtained by splitting cylinders, removing silica grains, homogenizing with an agate mortar, dispersing in ethanol, and depositing on copper grids; for SEM, embedded samples were polished (SiC grit 180–1000, then 15–3 µm diamond), oven-dried at 40 °C overnight, and carbon-coated; XRD used powders <50 µm; MIP samples (1–2 g core fragments) were vacuum-dried ≥7 days; micro-CT scans (CoreTOM) employed 120 kV, 28 W, 600 ms, 1 mm Al filter with ROI segmentation; carbonation depth was measured by EN 14630 phenolphthalein on freshly split faces; mechanical tests followed EN 1015-11 (flexural and compressive) at 28, 90, and 480 days.

summary: This clinical case series describes four pediatric patients with relapsed B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia after CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel) who were treated with inotuzumab ozogamicin (InO) and then underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. summary: This first-in-human phase I/II clinical study tested intra-arterial delivery of autologous mesoangioblasts to the tibialis anterior muscle in three m.3243A>G mitochondrial DNA mutation carriers, demonstrating safety with only mild, transient local adverse events and no vascular complications. Preliminary tissue analyses suggested mesoangioblast homing and early signs of regeneration, though evidence was inconclusive, supporting further evaluation with multiple dosing regimens.

summary: The authors present SPLONGGET, a single-cell long-read multiome method that integrates 10x Genomics barcoding with Oxford Nanopore sequencing to jointly profile whole-genome, chromatin accessibility, and full-length transcriptomes from thousands of cells while enabling targeted enrichment for deep single-cell genotyping. summary: The study shows that T cells from patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) exhibit mitochondrial depolarization and metabolic dysfunction across subsets, accompanied by epigenetic and signaling changes including reduced AMPK/autophagy and hyperactive Akt with increased glycolytic programming. Mouse model: leukemic splenocytes from aged Eμ-TCL1 mice were IV transferred into C57BL/6; for T-cell prep, spleens were mechanically homogenized to single-cell suspensions with RBC lysis, and T cells were activated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 Dynabeads plus 60 IU/mL recombinant human IL-2; idelalisib was added 1–2 hours post-activation and replenished every 2–3 days. summary: This article summarizes a European Medicines Agency-led Focus group that explored how to provide multistakeholder scientific advice for medicinal products used with medical devices and companion diagnostics under the EU MDR/IVDR framework. Reviewing nine case studies (four drug–device and five drug–CDx), the group identified question types suitable for joint advice, noted constraints on notified bodies’ involvement, and outlined options to improve coordinated evidence-generation planning without addressing clinical trial authorization topics.
summary_mandm: A Focus group comprising SAWP/CHMP experts, national competent authorities, notified bodies, industry, and EMA was formed to collect and analyze nine case studies; members worked in two break-out streams (drug–device and drug–CDx) to define question types suitable for multistakeholder advice and the expert mix required. The scope excluded clinical-trial/performance-study authorization, procedural/regulatory queries, and device classification, and acknowledged notified bodies’ legal limits on consulting; no biological samples, digestion, enzymes, buffers, temperatures, incubations, or mechanical processing were involved.

summary: The study identifies a public HLA class II–restricted neoantigen derived from the DNMT3A R882H hotspot mutation and a RUNX1 frameshift neoantigen that are recognized by CD4 T cells in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Monocyte-derived dendritic cells were generated 5 days with GM-CSF and IL-4, then matured 2 days with GM-CSF, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, PGE2, and IFN-γ; DCs were pulsed 4 h at 37°C with 100 nM peptides in IMDM + 2% FBS and co-cultured with naïve CD4 T cells (10:1) in IMDM + 5% HS + 5% FBS + IL-12 (10 ng/ml) + IL-2 (20 IU/ml), with IL-2 (100 IU/ml) and IL-15 (10 ng/ml) added on days 3 and 6. summary: The study introduces PB10X, a plate-based, 10X-compatible single-cell RNA-seq workflow that integrates barcoded template-switch oligos to enable early pooling and downstream use of standard 10X Single Cell 5' Gene Expression and V(D)J kits, while remaining compatible with Cell Ranger. raw_affiliation: Maastricht MultiModal Molecular Imaging Institute, Maastricht University, Maastricht, the Netherlands.
affiliation_notes: Institute extracted as the main institution; city and country directly mentioned.
summary: This study used spatial omics (MALDI-MSI-guided laser microdissection and label-free proteomics) to compare neocortex and hippocampus from temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) patients with PET-positive hypometabolism, PET-negative cases, and nonepileptic postmortem controls. PET-positive samples showed elevated phosphatidylserines, dysregulated calcium signaling, a neocortical shift from mitochondrial to cytosolic processes, and hippocampal disruptions in glycosylation and polyamine metabolism, suggesting distinct metabolic subtypes within TLE.
summary_mandm: Fresh-frozen human neocortex and hippocampus were collected intraoperatively from TLE patients, stored at −80°C, cryosectioned at 12 μm with a Leica Microsystems Cryotome, and mounted on ITO slides for lipid MALDI-MSI and on PEN membrane slides for proteomics. Norharmane matrix was applied with an HTX Technologies TM-sprayer; MALDI-MSI (Bruker rapifleX MALDI TissueTyper, negative mode, reflectron, 300–1600 m/z, 30×30 μm) guided region selection; post-MALDI sections were H&E stained, ROIs (~5 mm²) were excised by laser capture microdissection, and proteins were digested per a prior protocol (details not provided), peptides separated on a Thermo Scientific Dionex Ultimate 3000 UHPLC and analyzed on a Thermo Q Exactive HF in DIA mode; data were processed with SciLS, R, mmass, MATLAB, DIA-NN, and Perseus.
instrument: Leica Microsystems Cryotome; HTX Technologies TM-sprayer; Bruker rapifleX MALDI TissueTyper; laser capture microdissection system; Thermo Scientific Dionex Ultimate 3000 UHPLC; Thermo Scientific Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer

title: Towards implementing new payment models for the reimbursement of high-cost, curative therapies in Europe: insights from semi-structured interviews.
authors: Desmet, Thomas; Michelsen, Sissel; Van Den Brande, Elena; Van Dyck, Walter; Simoens, Steven; Huys, Isabelle
primary_topic: Health Systems, Economic Evaluations, Quality of Life
raw_affiliation: Clinical Pharmacology and Pharmacotherapy, Department of Pharmaceutical and Pharmacological Sciences, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium.
affiliation_notes: Institution name is clearly KU Leuven; city and country are explicitly mentioned.
summary: This qualitative study explored how to implement outcome-based spread payments (OBSP) for high-cost advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) in Belgium by interviewing 33 stakeholders and identifying necessary conditions such as pricing consensus, robust data infrastructure and financing, clear outcome-linked payment triggers, long-term follow-up, external governance, and transparency. It highlights barriers including administrative burden, fragmented data systems, accounting rule constraints, and lack of consensus, and proposes a framework of necessary and sufficient elements to guide practical OBSP adoption.
summary_mandm: A mixed-method design was used, building on a prior systematic review and roundtable discussions to develop a semi-structured interview guide. Purposeful maximum-variation sampling recruited 33 stakeholders (physicians, hospital pharmacists, hospital managers, policymakers, legislative and accounting experts, industry, patient representatives, sickness funds) who met inclusion criteria related to ATMP experience; interviews (~1 hour) were conducted in Dutch or English via Skype/telephone from July to October 2020, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, pseudonymized, and analyzed using framework analysis with deductive and inductive coding in NVivo (v20.4.1.851), yielding six thematic domains; ethics approval was obtained and two pilot interviews were included.

title: Treatment of patients with pMMR GI cancers with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL): a reality?
authors: Haanen, John B
raw_affiliation: Division of Medical Oncology, NKI, Amsterdam, Netherlands; Department of Medical Oncology, LUMC, Leiden, Netherlands; Oncology Service, CHUV, Lausanne, Switzerland. Electronic address: j.haanen@nki.nl.
affiliation_notes: AI cleaning failed: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'
summary: This Spotlight commentary reviews a Phase 2 trial showing that adoptive transfer of neoantigen-selected tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) is feasible in patients with refractory pMMR gastrointestinal cancers and yields durable responses, particularly when combined with anti-PD-1 therapy. While unselected TIL produced no RECIST responses, enrichment for neoantigen-specific TIL and combination with pembrolizumab improved objective response rates, highlighting the importance of tumor microenvironment and targeted TIL selection for efficacy.
summary_mandm: TIL therapy involved surgical resection of a metastatic lesion to harvest tumor tissue, in vitro culture and expansion of TIL, and a clinical regimen of lymphodepleting chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide plus fludarabine), TIL infusion, and high-dose IL-2; no tissue digestion enzymes, buffers, temperatures, or mechanical dissociation devices were specified. For the neoantigen-selected approach, whole-exome and RNA sequencing were used to predict neoantigens, dendritic cells were generated to present these antigens, TIL cultures were screened for neoantigen reactivity, and reactive TIL were expanded; the selection workflow extended the interval from resection to treatment to as long as 6 months. In an alternative arm, autologous peripheral blood T cells were engineered by γ-retroviral transduction of neoantigen-specific TCRs and infused; specific ex vivo activation reagents, media, incubation temperatures, or timing of culture were not detailed.
cell_selection_method: selection/enrichment of neoantigen-specific TIL using dendritic cell antigen presentation with reactivity screening of TIL cultures; expansion of reactive TIL
culture_timeframe: up to 6 months from tumor resection to infusion due to selection workflow; 2–3 weeks hospitalization for lymphodepletion, TIL infusion, and high-dose IL-2

summary: The study identifies and isolates heterotypic clusters of CD8+ T cells physically bound to tumor cells and/or APCs from all 21 human melanoma metastases examined, showing these clustered T cells are enriched for tumor-reactive and exhausted states with increased TCR clonality. T cells expanded from clusters exhibited markedly enhanced cytokine production and tumor killing ex vivo and improved tumor control in mouse models, indicating these commonly excluded cell clusters are a potent source of tumor-reactive T cells for therapeutic applications.

summary: This brief report shows that αβ T cells engineered with a high-affinity Vγ9Vδ2 TCR (TEGs) kill pediatric diffuse midline glioma (DMG) cells and that oncolytic adenovirus Δ24-RGD or reovirus R124 infection increases BTN3A (but not BTN2A1) expression on DMG cells. Under suboptimal γδ TCR ligand conditions (without pamidronate), combining TEGs with low-MOI oncolytic viruses additively enhances tumor cell killing, supporting a combination strategy for DMG therapy.
summary_mandm: Patient-derived DMG cultures (SU-DIPG-IV; VUMC-DIPG-G) were maintained at 37°C, 5% CO2 in Complete Tumor Stem Medium (TSM: 48% Neurobasal-A + 48% DMEM/F12 + 1% HEPES + 1% NEAA + 1% sodium pyruvate + 1% GlutaMAX; supplemented with 2% B27 (no vitamin A), EGF 20 ng/mL, bFGF 20 ng/mL, PDGF-AA 10 ng/mL, PDGF-BB 10 ng/mL, heparin 5000 U/mL, and pen/strep). For co-cultures, tumor cells were dissociated enzymatically with accutase (5 min), stained with CellTrace Violet, and seeded at 25,000 cells/well; infections used Δ24-RGD (MOI 5–50) or R124 (MOI 20–300) and were incubated 48 h in a 50/50 mix of TSM and RPMI + 10% FCS with or without pamidronate (30 µM). Human PBMCs (healthy donors) were preactivated with anti-CD3 (OKT3, 30 ng/mL) and IL-2 (50 IU/mL) in huRPMI (RPMI 1640 + GlutaMAX + 5% pooled heat-inactivated human serum + 0.5 M β-mercaptoethanol + pen/strep), retrovirally transduced twice within 48 h (pMP71 Vγ9Vδ2 TCR; Phoenix-Ampho with pHIT60 gag-pol and pCOLT-GALV env; 6 µg/mL polybrene), expanded with anti-CD3/CD28 Dynabeads and IL-2, and enriched by MACS (anti-αβ TCR biotin + anti-biotin MicroBeads; LD/LS columns); CD3, CD4, or CD8 subsets were positively selected as needed. Rapid expansion protocol used irradiated feeder PBMCs/Daudi/LCL-TM with IL-2 (50 IU/mL), IL-15 (5 ng/mL), and PHA-L (1 µg/mL); TEGs/LM1s were used 4–5 days post-stimulation. Co-cultures/infections ran 48 h; cells were harvested with accutase, stained (anti-CD3-AF700; 7-AAD), fixed in 4% PFA, and analyzed by flow cytometry; BTN3A1/2/3-PE and custom anti-BTN2A1-AF647 staining with Live/Dead Aqua assessed ligand expression; IFN-γ was quantified by ELISA (avidin-HRP/TMB).

title: Whole-body CD8+ T-cell PET imaging in patients with large B-cell lymphoma before and during CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy: a phase 2 study.
authors: De Boer, Janneke W; Keijzer, Kylie; Van Doesum, Jaap A; Smit, Nienke A M; Brouwers, Adrienne H; Van Sluis, Joyce; Lub-De Hooge, Marjolijn N; Pierik, Frank R; Huls, Gerwin A; Van Dijk, Lisanne V; Visser, Lydia; Diepstra, Arjan; Noordzij, Walter; Williams, Simon P; Ungewickell, Alexander; Elias, Sjoerd G; De Vries, Elisabeth G E; Niezink, Anne G H; Van Meerten, Tom
raw_affiliation: Department of Hematology, University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen, Groningen, the Netherlands. t.van.meerten@umcg.nl.

summary: This exploratory phase 2 single-arm clinical trial used 89Zr-labeled one-armed anti-CD8α antibody (89ZED88082A) PET to visualize whole-body CD8+ T-cell distribution in 23 patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma before and during CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel). Tumor uptake was heterogeneous, higher pre-CART uptake associated with higher early post-CART uptake and longer time to progression, no tracer-related adverse events were observed, and rapid tumor volume reduction was seen by day +7 post-infusion, underscoring the importance of a CD8-permissive tumor microenvironment.
summary_mandm: Patients underwent pre- and early post-infusion PET/CT imaging with 89ZED88082A (37 MBq, 10 mg; injected 2 days before imaging) using Biograph Vision Quadra, Vision 600, or Biograph mCT scanners with EARL-compliant reconstructions; [18F]FDG-PET/CT was used to assess metabolic tumor burden. Tumor lesions were delineated on 89ZED88082A-PET/CT aided by MUST-segmenter and RayStation, normal tissues were segmented with TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer, and partial volume corrections were applied; bridging therapy (including radiotherapy), apheresis (day −28), lymphodepleting chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide 500 mg/m2 and fludarabine 30 mg/m2 for 3 days), and axicabtagene ciloleucel infusion (day 0) followed standard practice. Tumor biopsies (ultrasound-guided when feasible) were formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded, subjected to autoradiography (phosphor storage plates; Typhoon imager) and IHC (Ventana Benchmark Ultra; anti-CD3, anti-CD8, anti-CD19; anti-Whitlow KIP1 for CAR), with CD8 density visually scored. Venous blood was processed for plasma and serum (stored at −80 °C) for cytokine profiling on the Ella Simple Plex platform, and gDNA was extracted from whole blood (QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit) for duplex qPCR quantifying FMC63 (CAR) and CD8 with GATA2 normalization using TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix and specified primer/probe sets and cycling conditions; no enzymatic tissue digestion was performed.

title: A bioengineering approach to guide non-integrated stem cell-derived embryo model towards yolk sac development and hematopoiesis.
authors: Shankar, Vinidhra; Zahmatkesh, Ensieh; Fuentes, Laury Roa; Trujillo, Fabiola Marques; Van de Wetering, Willine; López-Iglesias, Carmen; Caiment, Florian; Van Blitterswijk, Clemens; Vrij, Erik; Giselbrecht, Stefan

summary: The study establishes a chemically induced, non-integrated mouse stem cell-derived embryo model (XEn/EpiCs) that autonomously progresses in serum-free conditions to yolk sac-like vesicles exhibiting vasculogenesis, contracting cardiomyocyte niches, and blood island formation. A thermoformed milliwell platform enables continuous culture, live tracking, and pathway modulation (Wnt/BMP) to guide organogenesis and enhance yolk sac hematopoiesis.
summary_mandm: Mouse embryonic stem cells (Gata6:H2B:Venus) were expanded on MEFs in ES medium (DMEM high glucose + 10% FBS, LIF, CHIR99021, PD0325901) and passaged with Accutase for 3 min, then aggregated at 18–24 cells per microwell in 2.2% agarose hydrogel microwells and exposed for 24 h to XEn-induction (RF2C) factors (retinoic acid, FGF4 + heparin, CHIR99021, 8Br-cAMP, Y27632), after which cultures continued in advanced N2B27 (serum-free) up to day 14 in either suspension (transfer at 72 h) or thermoformed 800 µm milliwell arrays. For single-cell prep, day 10 structures were dissociated with TrypLE enzyme for 30 min at 37 °C (for scRNA-seq) or with Triple-E (Fisher Scientific #12563011) for ≥30 min with intermittent vortexing (for flow cytometry); viable cells (DAPI−) were FACS-sorted into Gata6:mVenus+ and − fractions. Immunostaining used 4% PFA fixation (30 min, RT), permeabilization (1% Triton X-100), blocking (2% BSA, serum, glycine, Triton X-100/Tween-20), primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, and secondary antibodies 3 h at 37 °C; paraffin sections underwent antigen retrieval at ~95 °C for 2–3 min. Functional assays included a FITC–dextran (4 kDa) diffusion test (2 mg/mL, 1.5 h) with optional EDTA (2 mM, 1.5 h on ice) to disrupt junctions, and cardiomyocyte stimulation with 20 µM DL-adrenaline for 1 h; BMP4, CHIR99021, or XAV939 were pulsed from 96–120 h to modulate pathways.

summary: The authors engineered tri-specific Wnt-IL-13 fusion proteins that co-activate Wnt/β-catenin and IL-13 signaling, thereby expanding human intestinal tuft cells and enhancing epithelial regeneration. title: A micro-CT-integrated 3D simulation framework reveals fluid transport mechanisms and void dynamics in root canal biomaterials.
authors: Raoof, Amir; Raoof, Maryam; Fathi, Hossein; Pouran, Behdad; Derakhshani, Reza
raw_affiliation: Department of Earth Sciences, Faculty of Geosciences, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands. r.derakhshani@uu.nl.
affiliation_notes: Extracted directly from 'Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands.' Department and email address ignored as per rules.
summary: The study introduces 3D-SALAM, a micro-CT–integrated computational framework that converts high-resolution scans of obturated human teeth into CFD models to mechanistically quantify void geometry, connectivity, and fluid transport. Proof-of-concept simulations show that hydrophilic surfaces and medium injection velocities maximize void saturation while applied pressure accelerates transport but increases spatial heterogeneity, highlighting a reproducible, non-destructive approach for evaluating root canal sealing performance and other porous biomaterials.
summary_mandm: Four recently extracted human single-rooted teeth were ultrasonically scaled, stored in isotonic saline, inspected at 20× magnification, decoronated at the CEJ with a high-speed diamond bur under water cooling, and instrumented using RaCe rotary files (sequence 40/0.10, 35/0.08, 25/0.04, 25/0.06, 30/0.06). summary: This methods paper describes a negative-selection FACS workflow that depletes CD90.2+ fibroblasts to generate highly enriched Schwann cell cultures from adult mouse sciatic nerves and brachial plexuses. summary: The study introduces AddGraft, a heterobifunctional PEG additive that integrates into (meth)acrylated hydrogels during photocrosslinking and enables subsequent, spatiotemporally controlled thiol-ene photografting of biochemical cues and crosslinkers without altering bulk mechanics. AddGraft supports high-resolution volumetric photopatterning, tunable local stiffening, and multi-compound grafting across GelMA, AlgMA, and PEGDA matrices while maintaining high hMSC viability and eliciting predictable cell morphological responses to dynamic mechanical modulation.
summary_mandm: AddGraft (acrylate–norbornene PEG) was synthesized via acryloylation of Boc-PEG1kDa-NH2, Boc deprotection with TFA, and norbornene installation using carbic anhydride; products were characterized by 1H/13C NMR. GelMA (DoM 60% or 80%) was prepared by reacting gelatin with methacrylic anhydride in CB buffer (pH 9, 50°C) with timed additions, neutralization (pH 7.4), dialysis (5 days, 4°C), sterile filtration, and lyophilization; AlgMA (DoF ~30%) was made by reacting alginate with methacrylic anhydride (pH ~7) for 3 days, precipitating in cold ethanol, drying, dialysis, and lyophilization; PEGDA (8 kDa) solutions were prepared at 4% w/v. Hydrogels (typically GelMA 5% w/v + LAP 0.1% w/v in PBS, AddGraft 0–10 mg/mL) were photocrosslinked using 405 nm light (Omnicure S2000 Elite) or a 365 nm CL-1000 UV crosslinker; volumetric printing used a Tomolite V2 (405 nm, 8.4 mW/cm²) with pre-cooling to 4°C and warming to 37°C post-print. For photografting, crosslinked gels containing AddGraft were infused with thiolated dyes or crosslinkers plus LAP (0.2% w/v) and, when needed, TEMPO (0.004–0.008% w/v) either overnight at 4°C (acellular) or 1 hour at 37°C (cell-laden), then irradiated (dose tests 50–2500 mJ/cm²; static 8–10 min UV) and washed in PBS up to 5 days; gradients and multi-compound grafting were achieved by programmed light-dose profiles. Photostiffening used DTT, SH-PEG2kDa-SH, or 8-arm PEG10kDa-SH at equimolar thiol:norbornene with LAP 0.2% w/v; AlgMA samples could be further stiffened with CaCl2 (50 mM, 2 h). summary: The study shows that circular mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) persists and becomes relatively enriched compared to nuclear DNA after decellularization of human and porcine livers and human veins, acting as a damage-associated molecular pattern that activates macrophages. summary: The study develops an injectable dual-network PVA/alginate hydrogel incorporating hydrothermally synthesized hydroxyapatite co-doped with copper and strontium, tuned by synthesis temperature to optimize crystallinity, mechanics, and bioactivity. summary: This study bioengineers human liver tissues by co-culturing intrahepatic cholangiocyte organoids with hepatic stellate cells and mesenchymal stromal cells in defined hydrogels, and shows that integrating mesenchymal cues, dynamic suspension culture, and a PIC-collagen hydrogel enhances tissue formation and hepatic maturation. summary: This study shows that azobenzene-functionalized, light-responsive liquid crystal polymer films can generate and erase microtopographies (pillars and grooves) in real time to provide reversible mechanical cues that modulate macrophage behavior in vitro. summary: The study uses microfluidic bioprinting to create a 3D in vitro thyroid model by printing alginate-based hydrogel fibers containing human thyroid cells, spheroids, and mouse embryonic stem cell-derived thyroid follicles, achieving precise structures with high cell viability and function. Mouse ESCs (A2Lox Nkx2-1-Pax8) were expanded on γ-irradiated MEFs in DMEM + 15% FBS + supplements (LIF 1000 U/mL, NEAA, sodium pyruvate, pen/strep, 2-mercaptoethanol), aggregated as hanging-drop EBs (4 days), embedded in Matrigel (50 µL drops) with doxycycline (3 days) then 8-Br-cAMP (14 days), and on the day of printing follicles were recovered from Matrigel by enzymatic digestion with Dispase II (10 mg/mL in HBSS) and Collagenase type IA (1.37 mg/mL in HBSS), followed by size filtration through 100 µm and 30 µm strainers. title: Modeling spheroid assembly dynamics and mechanical stress generation in magnetic-based biofabrication
authors: Guilliams, Maya; Ioannidis, Konstantinos; Dąbrowska, Karolina Z; Tosini, Marta; Lefas, Dimitrios; Serino, Gianpaolo; Sakellariou, Dimitrios; Papantoniou, Ioannis; Smeets, Bart

summary: The study combines experiments and an individual spheroid-based discrete element model to elucidate how magnetic forces, contact mechanics, and interfacial friction govern rapid assembly and stress generation in magnetized periosteum-derived cell spheroids. It shows that magnet geometry and spheroid number predict assembloid morphology (including ring-like patterns) and heterogeneous compressive stress distributions, enabling predictive control of tissue structure and mechanical microenvironments in magnetic biofabrication.
summary_mandm: Human periosteum-derived cells (hPDCs) were isolated from periosteal biopsies, expanded up to passage 9 at 37°C, 5% CO2, 95% RH in DMEM + 10% FBS + antibiotics + sodium pyruvate, detached with TrypLE Express, rinsed with PBS, and seeded into AggreWell 400 or 800 microwells pre-treated with anti-adherence solution to form spheroids. Spheroids were cultured for 3 or 7 days in chemically defined chondrogenic C8 medium (LG-DMEM, antibiotics, ascorbate-2-phosphate, dexamethasone, proline, ITS+ supplement, Y27632) supplemented with BMP-2, GDF5, TGF-β1, BMP-6, and FGF-2; high-purity Fe3O4 MNPs (30 µg Fe mL−1) were added for overnight incubation, after which spheroids were transferred to non-adherent 24-well plates and assembled for 60 s on a 3D-printed magnetic plate with cylindrical neodymium magnets (N45). Mechanical properties were measured via nanoindentation using an Optics11 Life Chiaro nanoindenter (49.5 µm spherical probe, 0.53 N/m cantilever) on poly-D-lysine–coated dishes in DPBS (displacement-controlled load-hold-unload protocol), and imaging/tracking quantified spheroid size, number, and radial velocities.

summary: This review provides a practical guide for experimental biologists on selecting and applying computational models to study stem cell differentiation, covering mechanistic ODE and abstract models, multiscale frameworks, and deep learning approaches. It links model choice to research questions and data types, outlines validation and risk mitigation, and illustrates use cases with hypothetical iPSC differentiation scenarios.

title: Multicellular microtissues from fused ligament- and bone-cell spheroids relevant to enthesis repair.
authors: Giacomini, Francesca; Anand, Shivesh; Vermeulen, Steven; Barata, David; Tahmasebi Birgani, Zeinab Niloofar; Emans, Pieter J; López-Iglesias, Carmen; Moroni, Lorenzo; Mota, Carlos; Giselbrecht, Stefan; Habibović, Pamela; Truckenmüller, Roman

summary: The study introduces a modular, scaffold-free platform that fuses patient-derived anterior cruciate ligament cell spheroids with osteogenically differentiated human mesenchymal stromal cell spheroids to generate microtissues modeling the ligament-to-bone enthesis. Spheroid maturation state controlled fusion dynamics and spatial organization (core-shell vs. juxtaposed), constructs expressed lineage markers with collagen X localized at the interface within 10 days, and acoustic stimulation (3 kHz) enhanced extracellular matrix deposition and growth, positioning the system for mechanobiology studies and therapeutic/micromaterial screening.
summary_mandm: Human ACL fibroblasts (from a 62-year-old donor) and bone marrow-derived hMSCs were expanded at 37°C, 5% CO2 in BML (DMEM high glucose, no sodium pyruvate, 10% FBS, 0.2 mM L-ascorbic acid 2-phosphate, penicillin/streptomycin) and BMB (α-MEM with GlutaMAX, 10% FBS, 0.2 mM L-ascorbic acid 2-phosphate, penicillin/streptomycin), respectively. Cells were aggregated (~500,000 cells per array) into spheroids for 48 h in non-adherent, Pluronic F108-treated polycarbonate microwell arrays (U-bottom, ~556 μm diameter, ~353 μm depth) and then differentiated: ACL spheroids in DML (BML + 0.01 μg/mL TGF-β3) for 7 or 21 days; hMSC spheroids in osteogenic medium (BMB + 10⁻⁸ M dexamethasone + 10⁻² M β-glycerophosphate) for 15 or 21 days; media changed every 2–3 days. For fusion, osteogenic spheroids were collected by gentle pipetting, centrifuged (300 rpm, 4 min), resuspended in BML, dispensed onto ACL spheroids, allowed to settle (37°C, 1 h), and co-cultured in DML with refresh every other day; aggregates were analyzed up to 10 days. Larger assemblies used agarose square milliwells (1 mm × 1 mm × ~0.44 mm) made by PDMS-stamp replica molding; pooled spheroids (50–100 per well) fused over 3 days. Acoustic stimulation employed a custom bioreactor (PMMA insert milled on Roland monoFab SRM-20; Diaphragm External Piezo Buzzer) delivering 3 kHz, 12 Vpp, 4 h/day for 7 days. Sample processing included fixation (4% PFA, 20 min RT), cryoembedding (15% sucrose/7.5% gelatin), cryosectioning (14 μm), permeabilization (0.1% Triton X-100), blocking (CAS-Block), overnight primary antibody incubation (4°C), secondary antibodies (2 h RT), mineral staining (OsteoImage), and confocal imaging; TEM used 1.5% glutaraldehyde in cacodylate buffer, osmium tetroxide/potassium ferrocyanide postfixation, ethanol dehydration, Epon embedding, ultramicrotomy, and uranyl acetate/lead citrate staining. No enzymatic tissue digestion for cell isolation was detailed in this manuscript.

authors: Mulders, Rick; Nickel-Maunu, Mathew; Van Hoolwerff, Marcella; Mazzini, Giorgia; Klomp, Lucas; Meijer, Hil; Post, Janine; Ramos, Yolande F M; Meulenbelt, Ingrid

summary: Using single-nucleus multiome (snRNA-seq + snATAC-seq) profiling across seven time points of a 49-day hiPSC chondrogenic differentiation, the authors mapped branching trajectories showing that chondrogenic fate emerges from a neurogenic program and bifurcates at day 21. title: Optimization of elastin proportion and crosslinking for collagen-elastin scaffolds as skin substitutes.
authors: Krymchenko, Roman; Kutluoğlu, Gizem Coşar; Manikowski, Dominique; Doberenz, Claudia; Boekema, Bouke K H L; Van Kuppevelt, Toin H; Daamen, Willeke F

summary: The study systematically optimized collagen-elastin dermal scaffolds by varying elastin content (5–20%), lyophilization method (room temperature vs. dehydrothermal, DHT), and EDC/NHS chemical crosslinking, and evaluated structural, mechanical, chemical, and biological properties including cytocompatibility. summary_mandm: Scaffolds were cast by dissolving soluble bovine elastin (0.08–0.32% w/v) in 0.25 M acetic acid (acidified to pH 3.5 with HCl), adding bovine collagen fibrils (1.28–1.52% w/v), homogenizing, pouring into 210 × 297 mm molds, and freeze-drying; lyophilization was performed either at room temperature or with dehydrothermal (DHT) treatment at 100°C. title: Osteoimmunomodulatory Stem Cell Nanoghosts as a Novel Nanotherapeutic for Bone Regeneration
authors: Micheli, Giovanni A; Yang, Tianyu; Gawlitta, Debby; Man, Kenny
journal: BioRxiv : the Preprint Server for Biology

summary: The study presents a bioengineered mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived nanoghost (NG) platform that overcomes extracellular vesicle scalability limitations and can be tuned by hypoxia and 3D GelMA culture to enhance osteoimmunomodulatory function. Freeze–thaw-produced NGs yielded far higher particle counts than a spin cup method and EVs, and NGs generated from hypoxia + 3D-preconditioned MSCs enriched anti-inflammatory cargo (notably IL-10), protected MSC viability, and partially restored osteogenic mineralization under IL-1β or TNF-α inflammatory challenge.
summary_mandm: ATDC5 and human bone marrow-derived MSCs were cultured (ATDC5 in DMEM/F-12 + 5% FBS; MSCs in α-MEM + 10% FBS + 0.2 mM L-ascorbic acid 2-phosphate + 1 ng/mL bFGF + antibiotics) and preconditioned for 48 h under normoxia (21% O2) or hypoxia (5% O2); MSCs were also encapsulated in GelMA hydrogels (5% or 15% w/v) with visible-light photoinitiators (1 mM Ru; 10 mM SPS) and photocrosslinked for 10 min at 30 mW/cm2. Additional processing included NG lysis with 0.1% Triton X-100 for ELISA, fluorescent staining for uptake assays, and osteogenic induction (α-MEM-based osteogenic medium with 10 mM β-glycerophosphate and 10 nM dexamethasone) with or without IL-1β or TNF-α.

summary: The study shows that human umbilical cord–derived mesenchymal stromal cells (UC-MSCs) remodel 3D skin-derived extracellular matrix hydrogels in a stiffness-dependent manner, contracting soft matrices and locally degrading stiff matrices to converge toward intermediate stiffness. summary: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on diagnosing and treating discogenic low back pain, highlighting MRI for screening and pressure-controlled provocative discography as the diagnostic reference, followed by a spectrum of conservative and interventional options. Thermal procedures include IDET (catheter heated to 90°C, ~14 min ramp then 4 min hold), biacuplasty/cooled RF (TransDiscal electrodes to 50–55°C with ~7–8 min ramp and ~7 min hold), PIRFT (70–90°C for 90–360 s), PRF of nucleus (~42°C; pulse settings e.g., 5–20 ms, 2–5 Hz, ~60 V for 15–20 min), ramus communicans RFA (e.g., 80°C for 120 s), basivertebral nerve ablation (85°C for 15 min), and SVN ablation (endoscopic guidance). summary: The study uses droplet-based microfluidics to encapsulate human corneal keratocytes in UPy-based supramolecular microgels that self-assemble into porous, biohybrid stromal microtissues supporting cell egress, migration, ECM deposition, and strong nuclear YAP activation. summary_mandm: PDMS droplet microfluidic devices (30 μm channels) were fabricated by soft lithography (SU-8 3000), PDMS (10:1) curing at 65°C for 3 h, plasma bonding to glass (Emitech K1050X), and fluorosilane treatment (5% silane in HFE-7500, 65°C). UPy monomers were prepared separately: M-type (UPy-Glycine + UPy-cRGD) at 2× final concentration dissolved at 70°C in NaOH/PBS (80 or 160 mM), neutralized with HCl and diluted in complete medium; B-type (UPy2-PEG10k) at 3× final concentration dissolved at 70°C in PBS for 1 h; both were UV-sterilized 20 min. Cells were added to the B-type solution (4000 cells/μL) and introduced into a pipette-tip-based microfluidic chip where M- and B-type streams met (aqueous flows 5 μL/min) and were sheared by HFE-7500 oil with 2.5% Pico-Surf (oil 10→30 μL/min) to form droplets; gelation proceeded 2 h at 37°C. Emulsions were broken (demulsified) with 20% PFO in HFE-7500; microgels were washed, counted, and cultured. HCKs were cultured in DMEM (high glucose), L-glutamine, 25 mM HEPES, 10% FBS, 1% P/S at 37°C, 5% CO2; detachment used trypsin (1:250) + 1 mM EDTA. Primary keratocytes were isolated from human corneal transplant leftovers, expanded in FBS-containing expansion medium (21% O2, 5% CO2), and detached with TrypLE Express; from day 5 they were either serum-activated to stromal fibroblasts (SFs) or switched to low-serum, high-glucose differentiation medium to generate corneal stromal keratocytes (CSKs). Cultures were maintained up to 21 days; immunostaining used 3.7% paraformaldehyde (20 min), 0.5% Triton X-100 (15 min), 10% serum blocking, primary antibodies overnight at 4°C, secondary antibodies 2 h at RT, and DAPI (1:250, 10 min). Mechanical processing also included syringe extrusion (30G) of fluorescent UPy-Cy3-labeled microgels to test injectability, with perimeter and eccentricity unchanged.

summary: The study presents a GMP-compliant, full 3D differentiation protocol for generating human pluripotent stem cell–derived islets and introduces a clinically applicable isopycnic density gradient centrifugation step to enrich endocrine cell–rich clusters without disrupting islet cytoarchitecture. Enriched clusters retained viability and function, showed improved endocrine composition, and matured further after transplantation into immunodeficient mice, supporting their potential for preclinical development of β cell replacement therapies.
summary_mandm: Human ESC/iPSC lines (HUES8, RC9, LUMC iPSC1–3) were expanded in antibiotic-free, animal component–free conditions (HUES8 on laminin-521; RC9/iPSCs on vitronectin) in Essential 8 medium, passaged with Versene, dissociated with Accutase, and seeded at 0.5×10^6 cells/ml into 125-ml spinner flasks or 30-ml disposable bioreactors on a magnet stir plate (60 rpm) at 37°C, 5% CO2, 100% humidity. Differentiation was initiated 48 hours after seeding and run as a seven-stage, ~30-day full 3D suspension protocol with daily media changes in stages 1–5 and every other day in stages 6–7. For enrichment, a continuous linear density gradient (1.045–1.100 g/ml) was formed in 50-ml tubes using UW solution (1.045 g/ml) and iobitridol (Xenetix) with computer-programmed peristaltic pumps; SC-islets were preincubated in UW for 30 min at 4°C, gently loaded atop the gradient, and centrifuged at 200g for 7 min (accel 7g, decel 3g) at 4°C. Seven equal-volume fractions were collected, gradient density validated with a DMA-35 N density meter, clusters recovered by passing through a 0.45 μm strainer, washed in islet medium to remove gradient components, and cultured individually in CMRL1066-based islet medium or stage 7 medium at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 day; fractions 2–5 were pooled as “enriched SC-islets” and fractions 1, 6, 7 as “depleted.”

authors: Wang, Peng; Zhang, Yang; Arntz, Onno J; Oliveira, Marina C; Yu, Taozhao; Yang, Zhihua; Van der Kraan, Peter M; Van Den Beucken, Jeroen J J P; Van de Loo, Fons A J

raw_affiliation: Department of Experimental Rheumatology, Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, the Netherlands.
summary: The study shows that collagen-binding properties distinguish two functional subpopulations of cow milk extracellular vesicles (EVs), with the collagen-binding fraction (cb+mEVs) enriched in Annexin V and driving osteogenesis in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo. Delivering cb+mEVs within collagen hydrogels enhanced bone regeneration in osteoporotic rat femoral condyle defects, while depletion of this subpopulation abrogated the effect.
summary_mandm: Cow milk EVs were isolated by sequential ultracentrifugation (70,000 g, 60 min, 4°C; remove fat/cells; Whatman #1/#50 filtration) followed by ultracentrifugation (110,000 g, 90 min, 4°C), PBS resuspension, 0.22 μm filtration, and size-exclusion chromatography on Sepharose CL-2B (fractions 4–5), with 0.22 μm re-filtration and storage at 4°C. Collagen-binding separation was performed by incubating fluorescently labeled EVs on type I collagen-coated plastic for 24 h at 4°C; unbound supernatant was collected as cb-mEVs, and bound cb+mEVs quantified by plate reader/IVIS. Immunomagnetic separation used protein A/G beads coated with anti-Annexin V antibody; mEVs were incubated 1 h at RT on a roller, beads washed with 0.5% Tween-20 PBS, AnxV-depleted supernatant collected, and bead-bound EVs eluted, using a DynaMag magnet. Collagen hydrogels (3 mg/mL) were formed by neutralizing acid collagen with NaOH and polymerizing 60 min at 37°C; EV release was assessed over 14 days, and residual gels digested with collagenase D (200 U/mL, 1 h, 37°C). summary: This multi-laboratory C4Bio study quantified methodological variability in uniaxial tensile testing of porcine aorta by comparing labs’ own protocols (round 1) versus a collaboratively developed consensus protocol using standardized tools (round 2). title: Designing Smartly: Understanding the Crystallinity of Melt Electrowritten Scaffolds.
authors: Zieliński, Piotr Stanisław; Zhang, Zhaohang; Squillante, Ilaria; Santiago, Guillermo Monreal; Koch, Marcus; Portale, Giuseppe; Kamperman, Marleen; Krushynska, Anastasiia; Włodarczyk-Biegun, Małgorzata Katarzyna
raw_affiliation: Polymer Science - Zernike Institute for Advanced Materials University of Groningen Groningen the Netherlands.
summary: This study shows that increasing collector speed during melt electrowriting of polycaprolactone scaffolds decreases fiber crystallinity and scaffold stiffness, as demonstrated by WAXS and tensile testing. A calibrated finite element model incorporating crystallinity-dependent bulk modulus and inter-fiber connection size accurately predicts tensile behavior across multiple scaffold architectures, guiding design for targeted mechanical properties.
summary_mandm: Scaffolds were fabricated by melt electrowriting using medical-grade PCL (PURASORB PC 12, Corbion) on a Spraybase The MELT A-1204-0001-01D printer, with designs generated via SEL Program Generator and parameters varied across voltage (4.5–6.0 kV), pressure (0.03–0.20 bar), collector speed (540–4800 mm/min), nozzle (0.3 mm), working distance (4 mm), temperature (100°C), and layers (typically 8); PCL was preheated 1 h and a sacrificial zone printed 3–5 min to stabilize the jet. Scaffolds were imaged by stereo microscopy (Nikon SMZ-2T with ToupCam) and SEM (gold-coated with JEOL JFC-1300; FEI Quanta 400 FEG), and tensile tests were performed (Instron 34SC-1KN, 5 N load cell, 5 mm/min) using microscope-guided cutting (~10×10 mm), paper-frame mounting with double-sided tape, and pneumatic clamps at 1 bar; WAXS (MINA diffractometer, Cu 1.5413 Å, Bruker Vantec 500, 80 mm sample-detector distance, 200–240 min acquisitions) provided crystallinity via Voigt peak fits (Fit2D and MATLAB), while inter-fiber connection footprints were measured after mechanically detaching fibers under a microscope. Finite element models (COMSOL Structural Mechanics) assumed ideal cylindrical fibers, linear elasticity, collector-speed-dependent bulk modulus and connection depth (0.5–1.5 µm), with mesh convergence and geometric nonlinearity; Young’s modulus was calibrated by optimization (Isight–MATLAB–COMSOL). No biological digestion, enzymatic steps, buffers, or incubation were used.

summary: This review synthesizes advances in granular hydrogels, focusing on how microgel design (size, shape, stiffness, packing, crosslinking) governs porosity, rheology, injectability/printability, degradability, and resultant biological responses in tissue repair and bioprinting. Assembly into granular hydrogels relies on physical packing (centrifugation, vacuum/gravity filtration, sedimentation, capillary wicking) and interparticle linking through covalent (photopolymerization, Michael addition, click reactions such as thiol‑ene, norbornene–tetrazine, azide‑alkyne), dynamic covalent (Schiff base/hydrazone), noncovalent (ionic gelation, guest‑host, metal–ligand, polyelectrostatic), or enzymatic crosslinking (e.g., FXIIIa; thrombin), with post‑printing/annealing by UV light, enzymes, or ionic baths; processing steps can include cooling/thermal gelation, dehydration/rehydration (lyophilization), and nozzle extrusion conditions that affect packing and porosity. summary: This study uses a high-throughput Double Orthogonal Gradient (DOG) PDMS platform to systematically screen how combinations of surface wrinkled topography, stiffness, and wettability affect human breast epithelial (MCF10a) and breast cancer (MCF7) cell behaviors. summary: This review evaluates human and rat renal proximal tubule in vitro models—spanning subcellular fractions, immortalized and primary cells, iPSC-derived cells/organoids, and microphysiological systems—for their transporter and metabolic enzyme expression/function to inform ADME and nephrotoxicity applications. It highlights strengths and limitations across culture conditions (plastic, filter inserts, microfluidic chips) and provides guidance on model selection for studying xenobiotic transport, metabolism, and clearance.

Primary PTEC isolation typically involves dissecting medulla from cortex, mincing cortex, collagenase digestion, sieving to separate glomeruli/tubular fragments (~65% proximal), optional density centrifugation, and seeding; ciPTEC proliferate at 33°C and are matured for ~10 days at 37°C, iPSC-derived proximal tubule-like cells are obtained by ~14-day differentiation (with one cryopreservation step possible using GW788388), and models are matured on filter inserts (apical/basolateral access) or microfluidic chips (ECM-coated channels; single or dual perfusion) under flow. Human MSCs were cultured in alpha-MEM + 10% heat-inactivated FBS + pen/strep + L-ascorbic acid-2-phosphate and exposed directly to nucleic acids/LNPs or to macrophage-conditioned media (first 2 days), then switched to osteogenic medium (alpha-MEM + 10% FBS + pen/strep + L-ascorbic acid-2-phosphate + 10 mM β-glycerophosphate + 10 nM dexamethasone); ALP was measured at days 4 and 10. summary: The study developed nanosized membrane particles derived from human adipose tissue mesenchymal stromal cell membranes and showed they reduce fibrosis markers and myofibroblast activation in a mouse unilateral kidney ischemia–reperfusion injury model and in human iPSC-derived kidney organoids. title: Microfluidic bioprinting as a tool to produce hiPSCs-derived renal organoids.
authors: Formica, Chiara; Addario, Gabriele; Fagiolino, Sveva; Moroni, Lorenzo; Mota, Carlos

summary: The study develops an automated microfluidic bioprinting approach to generate functional kidney organoids by combining hiPSC-derived metanephric mesenchyme and ureteric bud progenitors within core–shell filaments (gelatin core, alginate shell). The bioprinted organoids matured in vitro, showed renal segment markers, performed albumin uptake, and exhibited dose-dependent nephrotoxic responses to doxorubicin, demonstrating a scalable route to reproducible renal organoid production.
summary_mandm: hiPSCs (LUMC0031iCTRL08) were maintained on 1% Geltrex in mTeSR Plus at 37°C/5% CO2 and passaged with Accutase; cells were pretreated with 1% DMSO (24 h). For MM induction (adapted from Morizane), hiPSCs received CHIR99021 (8 µM) + noggin (5 ng/ml) in Advanced RPMI 1640 + 1% GlutaMAX for 4 days, followed by activin A (10 ng/ml) for 2 days, FGF9 (10 ng/ml) for 8 days, then basal medium to Day 20; for 3D MM, cells were lifted with Accutase at Day 4, pelleted (200 g, 4 min), reseeded in U-bottom ultra-low attachment plates (≥2×10^5 cells/well), and cultured with ROCKi (10 µM, removed after 24 h), activin A and FGF9, then FGF9 alone, then basal medium. For UB induction (adapted from Taguchi), hiPSCs received CHIR99021 + noggin (Days 0–2), then CHIR (1 µM), BMS 493 (0.1 µM), FGF9 (5 ng/ml), FGF1 (100 ng/ml), LDN-193189 (10 nM), heparin (1 nM) (Day 2–3), then CHIR (3 µM) plus the same factors plus GDNF (2 ng/ml) (Day 3–4); cells were lifted with Accutase at Day 4, aggregated in U-bottom plates (≥5×10^4 cells/well) with ROCKi overnight, then cultured with 10% Matrigel (Day 5), and from Day 6–10 in Adv RPMI + 1% GlutaMAX with 10% FBS, 10% Matrigel, BMS 493, R-Spondin-1 (100 ng/ml), FGF1 (100 ng/ml), LDN-193189 (10 nM), GDNF (2 ng/ml), and KGF/FGF-7 (30 ng/ml). For MM+UB organoids, Day 4 MM and UB single cells were combined 1:1 (≥2×10^5 cells/well), pelleted (200 g, 4 min), and cultured in Adv RPMI + GlutaMAX with Y-27632 (24 h), activin A, BMS 493, FGF9, LDN-193189, GDNF, and heparin to Day 6, then without Y-27632 and activin A to Day 14, and basal medium to Day 20+. Microfluidic bioprinting used an Aspect Biosystems RX1 with a TP245 CENTRA core–shell printhead: core bioink contained Day 5 MM+UB single cells (18×10^6 cells/ml) in 1% gelatin + 1% Geltrex in Adv RPMI + 1% GlutaMAX + 10 µM Y-27632; shell ink was 0.75% alginate in TBS; crosslinker was 125 mM CaCl2 with 8% PVA in TBS; channels ran at 100 mbar; filaments (~20 mm) were cultured with FGF9, activin A (first 24–48 h), LDN-193189, heparin, GDNF, BMS 493, with Y-27632 for 24 h, then to Day 14, then basal to Day 20+. Whole-mount IF used 4% PFA fixation (40 min RT), permeabilization with 0.1% Triton X/PBS (15 min), blocking (2 h, 10% serum, 1% Triton X, 0.05% Tween-20), overnight primary at 4°C, extensive washes, overnight secondary at 4°C, and DAPI; Albumin-FITC uptake was done at 0.5 mg/ml for 24 h at 37°C (4°C control). Doxorubicin nephrotoxicity assays used 2 or 10 µM for 48 h; RNA was extracted with TRIzol and analyzed by qRT-PCR.

title: Modulating adipose-derived stromal cells' secretomes by culture conditions: effects on angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and immunomodulation.
authors: Pinheiro-Machado, Erika; Koster, Claudia C; Smink, Alexandra M
raw_affiliation: Department of Pathology and Medical Biology, University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Groningen, Netherlands.

summary: This study evaluates how different culture conditions (normoxia, cytokines, high glucose, hypoxia, and hypoxia + high glucose) modulate human and rat perirenal adipose-derived stromal cell (ASC) secretomes and how these secretomes affect angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and humoral alloimmunity in vitro. Normoxia- and hypoxia-derived secretomes consistently enhanced tube formation, collagen deposition, and immunomodulation, whereas high glucose and cytokine-conditioned secretomes had weaker or more variable effects, with human high glucose secretomes impairing collagen deposition.
summary_mandm: Human and rat perirenal adipose tissue was washed, minced, and digested with collagenase neutral protease blend 4 (0.5 mg/mL; Nordmark) in serum-free DMEM (STD-M (-)) at 37°C while shaking for 30 min, followed by centrifugation (700 × g, 7 min, RT) to separate stromal cells; cells were cultured in DMEM + 10% FBS (STD-M (+)) and passaged at ~80% confluence. Secretomes were generated by seeding prASC (50,000 cells/well, 6-well plates), serum-starving overnight in STD-M (-), then culturing 72 h under normoxia (21% O2) or hypoxia (1% O2) in STD-M (-), Cyto-M (-) (DMEM + IFN-γ 20 ng/mL, TNF-α 21.5 ng/mL, IL-1β 10 ng/mL), or high glucose DMEM (35 mM) for high glucose and hypoxia + high glucose conditions; supernatants were cleared (2,500 × g, 10 min), pooled, snap-frozen, and stored at −80°C. RAEC were isolated by placing 2 mm aorta explants intima-down on Cultrex BME, expanding outgrowth in EBM-2 (+), and releasing cells with dispase II (60 min, 37°C); HUVEC (Lonza) were expanded in EBM-2 (+). Tube formation assays used Matrigel-seeded HUVEC/RAEC (35,000 cells/well) plus secretomes for 18 h at 37°C. Rat dermal fibroblasts were obtained by serial explant culture after digesting the epidermis with collagenase I (0.3%, Sigma) in a 37°C water bath for 30 min; human fetal lung fibroblasts (FLF92) were cultured in DMEM/F12. For collagen assays, fibroblasts were serum-starved in STD-M (-) then exposed to secretomes for 72 h, fixed in cold methanol (−20°C, overnight), stained with Picrosirius-Red, washed with 0.1% acetic acid, dye eluted in 1 M NaOH, and OD measured at 540 nm. One-way MLRs (7 days, 37°C, 5% CO2) were performed with mismatched donors ± secretomes; resulting supernatants (alloantibodies) were applied to resting PBMC/splenocytes, then rabbit complement added for 2 h (after 30 min preincubation) and survival quantified by WST-1.

summary: This study engineers a library of gelatin and GelMA bioresins by tuning molecular weight and degree of modification to enable high-fidelity, multi-material volumetric bioprinting (VBP) and a plug-and-play suspension bath for embedded extrusion volumetric printing (EmVP). authors: Dudaryeva, Oksana Y; Buchholz, Maj-Britt; Größbacher, Gabriel; Amaral, Sofia; Florczak, Sammy; Bonhomme, Camille; Ferrer, Alvaro Rojo; Tibbitt, Mark W; Levato, Riccardo

summary: The study integrates volumetric bioprinting with photopolymerization-induced phase separation of gelatin–norbornene/PEG hydrogels to create centimeter-scale constructs with hierarchical porosity (printed mm-scale channels and intrinsic micron-scale pores). summary: This review synthesizes how human endometrial epithelial organoids recapitulate the structure, transcriptomics, hormone responsiveness, and functions of the native endometrium, enabling mechanistic studies of receptivity, ion-channel signaling, and disease. summary: This scoping review analyzes 1,722 publications (2010–2025) on human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte differentiation to assess how oxygen conditions are handled and reported. title: Photo-Cross-Linked Porous Hybrid Networks Based on Insoluble Collagen and Poly(trimethylene carbonate).
authors: Van Bochove, Bas; Van Dommelen, Lieke H A; Macarez, Anne-Constance; Ankoné, Marc; Versteeg, Elly M M; Van Kuppevelt, Toin H; Daamen, Willeke F; Poot, André A; Grijpma, Dirk W
raw_affiliation: Advanced Organ bioengineering and Therapeutics, Department of Bioengineering Technologies, Techmed Centre, University of Twente, Enschede 7522 NB, The Netherlands.
summary: The study fabricates highly porous, photo-cross-linked hybrid networks from methacrylated insoluble type I collagen (ICol-MA) and methacrylated poly(trimethylene carbonate) (PTMC-tMA), yielding scaffolds with high gel content and improved mechanical properties relative to collagen-only or non-cross-linked controls. It further shows that solvent choice critically affects collagen fibril structure and mechanics, with acetic acid preserving collagen banding and providing tougher collagen networks than DMSO/HCl, underscoring the need to optimize solvent effects for hybrid scaffold performance.
summary_mandm: Insoluble bovine type I collagen fibrils (ICol) were methacrylated by reacting a 0.5% (w/v) ICol dispersion in 0.25 M acetic acid with glycidyl methacrylate (10 mL/g) for 1 day at room temperature in the dark, followed by dialysis (0.25 M acetic acid 24 h; then water 2 days) and freeze-drying to yield ICol-MA (DF ~24%). A three-armed PTMC oligomer was synthesized by ring-opening polymerization of trimethylene carbonate at 130 °C for 3 days with TMP initiator and Sn(Oct)2 catalyst, then methacrylated in dry DCM using methacrylic anhydride and triethylamine (7 days, RT, dark) with hydroquinone inhibitor to produce PTMC-tMA (DF ~96%). Non-cross-linked collagen scaffolds were made by swelling ICol (0.8% w/v) in 0.25 M acetic acid at 4 °C for 16 h, homogenizing with a Potter−Elvehjem homogenizer, freezing (−20 °C), and freeze-drying. EDC/NHS cross-linking used pre-equilibration in 50 mM MES buffer (pH 5.0) with 40% ethanol for 30 min at RT, then 4 h in 50 mM MES containing 33 mM EDC and 6 mM NHS, followed by sequential washes (0.1 M Na2HPO4 ×2; 1 M NaCl ×2; 2 M NaCl ×2; water ×6) and freeze-drying. Photo-cross-linked collagen networks were prepared by dispersing ICol-MA at 3% (w/v) in DMSO/HCl (theoretical pH ~2), homogenizing, adding Irgacure-2959 (6 wt% of ICol-MA), casting, freezing at −25 °C overnight, and UV-irradiating at 365 nm for 1 h on a −15 °C plate while frozen; solvent exchange was performed by gradually adding water (~1 mL/min for 24 h) to replace DMSO/HCl, then freezing (−25 °C) and lyophilizing; an alternative used 0.25 M acetic acid (0.9% w/v ICol-MA) with the same UV protocol. PTMC networks were formed by dissolving PTMC-tMA (15% w/v) in DMSO/HCl at 70 °C for 24 h, adding Irgacure-2959 (1 wt% of PTMC-tMA), casting, freezing (−25 °C), UV (365 nm, 1 h, −15 °C), solvent exchange, and lyophilization. Hybrid networks were made by mixing equal volumes of ICol-MA dispersion (6% w/v stock) and PTMC-tMA solutions (10% or 30% w/v) in DMSO/HCl to obtain final 3% ICol-MA with 5% or 15% PTMC-tMA; photoinitiator was added (6 wt% relative to collagen; 1 wt% relative to PTMC), followed by casting, freezing, UV cross-linking, solvent exchange, and freeze-drying. Mechanical processing included homogenization with a Potter−Elvehjem homogenizer; key temperatures were −25 °C freezing, −15 °C UV cross-linking plate, and 70 °C PTMC dissolution; buffers included 50 mM MES (pH 5.0) with 40% ethanol for EDC/NHS cross-linking; no enzymatic digestions were used.

summary: The study presents a hyaluronic acid hydrogel crosslinked via SPAAC with a photolabile o-nitrobenzyl PEG crosslinker that enables rapid gelation, tunable stiffness, and on-demand photodegradation for cell recovery. summary: The study shows that cooperative multivalent binding and receptor clustering at biointerfaces arise when both ligands on supramolecular polymers and receptors in supported lipid bilayers share matched dynamics, enabling a clustered (type-II) anchoring mode. summary: The study reports the synthesis of a curcumin–polycaprolactone block copolymer (MCP) via ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone using maleic anhydride–modified curcumin, with structural confirmation by FTIR, 1H NMR, UV–Vis, and DSC. MCP exhibited enhanced antioxidant activity, UV-blocking, electrospinnability, and biocompatibility, supported fibroblast migration, and, when incorporated into PVA films with Cu or Fe, showed selective anti-Pseudomonas activity without systemic or contact toxicity in Galleria mellonella.
summary_mandm: Maleic anhydride–modified curcumin (MC) was synthesized by dissolving curcumin and maleic anhydride (1:1 molar) in THF, refluxing at 65°C for 12 h, and drying by rotary evaporation at 40°C. MCP was prepared by ring-opening polymerization: MC in THF was combined with ε-caprolactone and Sn(Oct)2 (0.1 g/mL in toluene), reacted under N2 at 80°C for 12 h, dissolved in DCM, precipitated with cold diethyl ether twice, and vacuum-dried; MCP–Cu/Fe complexes were formed by dissolving metal salts in MeOH, mixing with MCP (MeOH, sonication), adjusting pH (Cu: NaOH to ~5; Fe: HCl to ~3), stirring 1 h, precipitating with ether, centrifuging, washing with MeOH, and drying. summary: The study synthesizes a series of ureidopyrimidinone (UPy) monomers with varying alkyl spacer lengths and shows how hydrophobicity tunes their supramolecular polymerization, dynamics, morphology, pH/thermal responsiveness, and gel mechanics in water.
